unit.title: Reading a company's accounts
unit.description: Price and value, income statement, balance sheet, cash, debt and quarterly results

u16l1.title: Price and value aren't the same

texts: What you pay and what you get
A company earns **€2** per share a year and you decide how much to pay for it. How many years of earnings does it take to get the price back?
You pay €40 for the share and its earnings grow 5 % a year. In how many years do the earnings add up to what you paid?
In about 5 years
In about 15 years
In about 40 years
Adding up its earnings, which grow 5 % a year, it takes you **15 years** to reach €40.
Without touching the growth, find the highest price at which you get it back in 10 years.
At **€25** you get it back in 10 years; at €80, in 23. **Price is what you pay and value is what you get**: the same company can be a good buy at one price and a bad one at another.
You're paying so much it would take decades to get it back.
Growing like that for years on end? Very few companies manage it.
Now that's a reasonable price for what it earns!
Move the price and see how many years it takes
Meet Mr Market
Mr Market
Benjamin Graham pictured the market as a moody business partner who offers you a price every day.
I'm feeling euphoric today! I'll buy your stake for €40. Tomorrow, who knows.
A week later, without the business changing at all…
Everything's going terribly. I'll sell you my stake for €12. Quick!
You estimate the company is worth about €20 a share. What do you do?
Sell: if he's scared, something must be about to happen
You'd be selling cheap just when the business hasn't changed.
Check the business is still the same and, if so, buy
That's it: the price has dropped, the value hasn't. His price is an offer, not an order.
Buy with all your money without checking anything
Good instinct, but check your estimate and don't put everything in.
At €12, something worth €20: a **40 %** margin of safety.

steps.title: Margin of safety
steps.body:
«Price is what you pay; value is what you get» (Warren Buffett).

**Fundamental analysis** studies the business (sales, profits, debt, competition) to estimate what it's **worth**: it answers *what* to buy. **Technical analysis** studies the chart and tries to answer *when*.

If you estimate a share is worth €20 and you'll only buy it below €15, you have a **25 % margin of safety**: a cushion in case your estimate is wrong.
steps.key: An excellent company bought too expensively can be a bad investment.
steps.tip: Value is an estimate; that's why you need a cushion.

texts: From sales to profit
Panadería Global is a made-up company (figures in **millions of euros**). Is each item income, an expense or neither?
Profit before tax
Income
Expense
Neither
Sales of bread and pastries
It's the first line of the account: sales.
Flour, butter and so on (cost of sales)
Taking it away leaves the **gross margin**: 400, or 40 %.
Salaries, rent and electricity (operating expenses)
Taking them away leaves **EBITDA**: 200.
A new bank loan
Borrowing isn't earning: it's debt, and it goes on the balance sheet.
Wear and tear on the ovens (depreciation)
It's not a payment this year, but the ovens wear out. That leaves **EBIT**: 150, or 15 %.
Interest on the debt
After paying it, 130 is left before tax.
Place the six items.
Costs are taken away one by one: gross margin, EBITDA, EBIT and **130 before tax**. After paying 25 % in tax, **€97.5m** of net profit is left: with 100 million shares, EPS of €0.975.
Hint: has that money been earned or just borrowed?
Nice! Watch the bottom line shrink.
Income, expense or neither? Place each item
More sales, more profit?
Carla
My favourite company has sold loads more this year. I'm buying!
But its costs have risen faster than its sales.
What do you check before buying?
Nothing: if it sells more, it earns more
Not always: if costs rise faster, the **margin** shrinks.
The margins and how they're changing
That's it! The **trend** in margins matters more than any one year's figure.
Just this year's profit
Better, but a single year can mislead. Look at several.
A real case: Inditex sold €38,632m in its 2024 financial year.
Gross margin of 57.8 % and €5,866m of profit: more than €15 for every 100.
It's a figure to practise with, not a recommendation.

steps.title: Margins and EPS
steps.body:
• **Gross margin:** high (60-80 %) in software or luxury; low (20-30 %) in supermarkets.
• **Operating margin** (EBIT ÷ sales): how efficient the business is.
• **Net margin:** what's left for shareholders.
• **EPS** (earnings per share): net profit ÷ number of shares.
steps.key: Revenue is vanity, profit is sanity and cash is reality.

texts: What it owns and what it owes
Panadería Global's balance sheet, in **millions of euros**. Place each item: is it something it **owns** or something it **owes**?
Equity
What it owns (assets)
What it owes (liabilities)
Cash in the bank
Money is the most liquid thing it has.
Ovens and shops
They belong to it and help it make and sell.
Bank loans and bonds
It's financial debt: it has to be paid back with interest.
What customers owe it and the flour in the storeroom
Receivables and stock: assets that will soon be money.
Unpaid supplier invoices
What it hasn't paid yet is debt too.
The «Panadería Global» brand
A well-known brand is an asset too.
Place the six items and find out the equity.
**Assets = liabilities + equity**: 1,000 = 550 + 450. With 100 million shares, book value is **€4.5** per share.
Hint: what you haven't paid yet is debt too.
Going well! What's at the bottom is what's left for shareholders.
Owns it or owes it? Place each item
Two bakeries and a crisis
Sofía
Two bakeries earn the same. Bakery A owes €50m and has €300m of equity. Bakery B owes €400m and has €50m.
If they earn the same, it doesn't matter which one I buy, right?
A crisis hits and sales at both fall 30 %.
Which one suffers more?
Bakery A
With so little debt, A can ride out several bad years.
Bakery B: its interest bill is still there even if it sells less
Exactly: debt doesn't wait for the good times to come back.
Both the same: they earned the same
In the good years, yes. In the bad ones, debt makes the difference.
Debt doesn't sink a company in the good years, but in the bad ones.

steps.title: A snapshot, not a film
steps.body:
The balance sheet is a **snapshot** on a specific day; the income statement is the **film** of the whole year. You need to look at both.

Panadería Global's liquidity: short-term assets (80 + 170 = **250**) against short-term debts (**150**): it covers them.
steps.key: What a company owns is funded either by debt or by shareholders' money.

texts: Profit isn't cash
A year at Obrador Luna, another made-up company (in **millions of euros**): it has sold 100, but hasn't been paid for all of it. What really moves its cash?
Cash for the year
Cash in
Cash out
No cash movement
Sales already paid for
Money that's already in the bank.
Sales it will be paid for next year
They count towards this year's profit, but the money hasn't arrived yet.
Salaries, flour and rent, already paid
An expense and a payment at the same time: cash goes out.
Depreciation of the ovens
It's deducted from profit, but it isn't a payment.
Buying a new oven
It's investment (*capex*): cash goes out, even though it's not an expense for the year.
Place the five items.
Its income statement shows **+10** of profit (100 − 80 − 10), but its cash shows **−30**. Profit is an accounting opinion; **cash is a fact**.
Hint: has money come into or gone out of the bank this year?
See? Selling isn't the same as getting paid.
Cash in, cash out or no movement? Place each item
A company that grows… without getting paid
Marina
This company is growing 30 % in sales and profits. It's a machine!
But what its customers owe it has tripled, and its free cash flow has been negative for three years.
What do you do?
I buy: it's growing like crazy
Growing sales without collecting the money is exactly the red flag.
I find out why it isn't getting paid before buying
Good. Gowex and Wirecard had brilliant figures that never reached the bank.
I buy a little, just in case
If the figures aren't real, that little bit is lost too.
Enron, Wirecard and Gowex reported profits that never turned into cash.
If profits never reach the bank account, don't trust the profits.

steps.title: The three parts of cash flow
steps.body:
1. **Operating:** the money the business generates day to day.
2. **Investing:** ovens, shops, buying other companies (*capex*).
3. **Financing:** debt taken on or paid back, dividends and share buybacks.

**FCF = operating cash flow − capex.** Panadería Global generates €160m and invests €60m: **FCF of €100m**, €1 per share. That's what it can pay out, use to buy back shares or use to cut debt without harming the business.
steps.key: Profit is an accounting opinion; cash is a fact.

texts: Working out net debt
To find out how much Panadería Global really owes, you take its cash away from its financial debt. Figures in **millions of euros**.
Net debt
Financial debt
Cash
Doesn't count
Bank loan
Debt with interest: it counts.
Money in the bank
It could use it to pay back debt: it's subtracted.
Unpaid supplier invoices
It's trade debt, from day-to-day business: net debt only looks at financial debt.
Bonds issued
It's financial debt too: it has to be paid back with interest.
Ovens and shops
It's something it owns, not debt or cash.
Place the five items and work out its net debt.
**Net debt = financial debt − cash**: 400 − 80 = **€320m**. With EBITDA of 200, that's **1.6 times**: comfortable, below 2.
Hint: only debt that pays interest counts.
Nice! Cash is subtracted: it could use it to pay.
Debt, cash or doesn't count? Place each item
The crisis hits
Jorge
My company owes €600m net and makes €200m of EBITDA. Three times: acceptable.
A crisis hits. EBITDA falls to €120m; the debt stays the same.
What happens to its net debt/EBITDA?
It stays at 3: it hasn't borrowed more
The debt doesn't change, but EBITDA does: 600 ÷ 120 = **5 times**.
It rises to 5: from acceptable to worrying
That's it! Without borrowing a single euro more, the debt weighs much more.
It falls, because it earns less
The other way round: with less EBITDA, it would take more years to pay it off.
And the interest still has to be paid…
That's why debt sinks companies in the bad years.

steps.title: How much is too much?
steps.body:
**Net debt / EBITDA:** under 2, comfortable; over 4, worrying. It depends on the sector: utilities, toll roads and property companies can carry more debt because their income is very stable.

**Interest cover** (EBIT ÷ interest): Panadería Global, 150 ÷ 20 = **7.5 times**. Below 2-3, any stumble starts to hurt.

If cash is bigger than debt, there's **net cash**: Inditex ended its 2024 financial year with €11,495m.
steps.key: Debt multiplies: the good years look better and the bad ones, much worse.

texts: A record nobody liked
Nora
12 March 2025. Inditex reports its results.
Record profit: €5,866m, up 9 %! The share price is bound to go up.
What do you think the share did that day?
It rose sharply: it's a record
It fell more than **7 %**: it was its slowest growth since 2020.
It fell: the market expected more
That's it! It fell more than 7 %: the market was underwhelmed.
It didn't move
It moved, and a lot: more than 7 % down.
The market doesn't compare with last year: it compares with **what it expected**.
That average of what analysts expect is called the **consensus**.
Surprise or disappointment
Results day: what matters is the **gap with what was expected**. What does the share usually do in each case?
Tends to rise
Tends to fall
EPS of €1.10 when the consensus expected €1.20
It's compared with what was expected, not with last year.
It loses money, but much less than expected
A positive surprise can be celebrated even with losses.
Record profit, but below the consensus
Like Inditex in 2025: the record was already in the price.
It raises its forecasts for the rest of the year
What's coming usually matters more than the quarter just ended.
It hits its numbers for the quarter, but cuts its guidance
Cutting what it forecasts for the coming quarters usually weighs heavily.
Better margins than expected
Anything that improves what's expected for the future pushes it up.
Sort the six results.
The price reacts to the **gap between what happens and what was expected**. And what the company forecasts, its *guidance*, usually matters more than the quarter that has just ended.
Hint: don't ask whether it's good, but whether it's better than expected.
Nice! What's expected is already in the price.
Up or down? Sort each result

steps.title: Gap days
steps.body:
Four times a year, listed companies publish their accounts. Beforehand, analysts publish their forecasts (sales, EPS and what they expect for the future): their average is the **consensus**.

These are days of **price gaps**: the share can open far from the previous close, and a stop is triggered at the first available price, maybe well below where you planned.
steps.key: In the stock market, good news that was already expected isn't news.

u16l7.title: Reading an annual report without getting lost

texts: Signals in an annual report
An annual report can run to 300 pages. These things are quick to spot: are they a **red flag** or a **good sign**?
Red flag
Good sign
The auditor gives a qualified opinion
The auditor isn't comfortable with something in the accounts.
Free cash flow keeps pace with profit
Profits turn into real money.
Three different auditors in four years
Changing auditors that often can hide disagreements.
Auditor's report with no qualifications
It says the accounts give a true and fair view.
«Adjusted» profit very different from the official figure, year after year
If there are «one-offs» every year, they aren't one-offs.
Sales and profit growing five years in a row
A long trend says more than a single snapshot.
Sort the six signals.
The **auditor** tells you whether the accounts are reliable, and **cash** whether the profit is real. And compare at least 5 years: a single snapshot can mislead.
Hint: do the numbers add up, or is someone dressing them up?
Nice! You're reading a report like an analyst now.
Red flag or good sign? Sort each one
The CEO's letter
CEO
A historic year! Exceptional growth and a bright future.
In the notes: debt has doubled and «adjusted» profit has been stripping out «exceptional» costs for three years.
What do you give more weight to?
The letter: nobody knows the company better
The letter is the story; the notes are the facts. And they don't match.
The notes and the cash
Good: the numbers in the notes don't come with adjectives.
Both equally
When they don't match, the facts win: notes and cash.
Always compare adjusted profit with the official figure and with cash.
Enthusiasm doesn't pay off debt.

steps.title: Where everything is
steps.body:
The important parts: **financial statements** (income statement, balance sheet and cash flows), **notes** (debt, lawsuits, adjustments), the **auditor's report** (check it has no «qualifications»), **risks** and the letter from the chair or CEO, which is the story.

Where: the **investor relations** website, the **CNMV** (Spanish listed companies) and **SEC EDGAR** (US: annual **10-K** and quarterly **10-Q**). Compare at least **5 years**.
steps.key: Read the numbers and the notes first; the story, afterwards.

u16l1-1.prompt: What does fundamental analysis try to answer?
options: What to buy and whether it's expensive or cheap
u16l1-1.explanation: Technical analysis tries to answer when; fundamental analysis, what and at what price.

u16l1-2.prompt: You estimate a share is worth €40 and it's trading at €30. What margin of safety do you have on the estimated value?

u16l1-3.prompt: You want a 30 % margin of safety on an estimated value of €50. Below what price would you buy?

u16l1-6.prompt: The gap between the estimated value and the price you pay is called the margin of ____.
u16l1-6.explanation: It protects you if your estimate is wrong.

u16l1-7.prompt: Is it about price or value?
options: The company will generate about €100m of cash a year
It has a brand that lets it raise prices
u16l1-7.explanation: You see the price on the screen; the value comes from analysing the business.

u16l1-9.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: Sure, it's already hit the floor
Buy twice as much to average down
First look at why it fell and what the business is worth: cheap isn't the same as undervalued
u16l1-9.explanation: A low price is only an opportunity if it's below the value.
feedback: Something that's fallen 60 % can fall another 60 %.
Doubling up without analysing is just betting more blindly.
OK… and what if it fell because the business is broken? Then the value fell too.
lines: This share has fallen 60 %, it can't go any lower!

u16l2-1.prompt: Put the income statement in order from top to bottom.
u16l2-1.explanation: Costs, depreciation, interest and tax are deducted one by one.

u16l2-2.prompt: EBITDA is earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and ____.
u16l2-2.explanation: It measures what the business earns before how it's financed and before the wear and tear on its assets.

u16l2-3.prompt: Sales of €500m and cost of sales of €300m. What's the gross margin?

u16l2-4.prompt: Net profit of €60m and 40 million shares. What's the EPS?

u16l2-5.prompt: Inditex had sales of €38,632m and earned €5,866m in its 2024 financial year. What was its net margin? (one decimal place)

u16l2-6.explanation: It measures how much operating profit each euro of sales leaves behind.

u16l2-9.prompt: This is the real price of a share over two months. What trend does it show? (Apple · closes every 3 sessions · March–May 2026)
u16l2-9.explanation: In the short term, prices are driven by expectations; in the long term they tend to follow profits. The income statement tells you whether there are profits behind the rise.

u16l3-1.prompt: Match each concept with its definition.
u16l3-1.explanation: Assets = liabilities + equity: it always balances.

u16l3-4.prompt: A company has assets of €800m and liabilities of €500m. What's its equity?

u16l3-5.prompt: Equity of €450m and 100 million shares. If the share trades at €15, how many times its book value are you paying?

u16l3-6.prompt: Order from most to least liquid (easiest to turn into money first).
u16l3-6.explanation: Cash is already money; a factory can take years to sell.

u16l3-7.prompt: Short-term assets of €250m and short-term debts of €300m. What does it indicate?
options: It could struggle to pay what falls due soon
u16l3-7.explanation: What falls due within the year is more than what it can turn into money within the year.

u16l3-9.prompt: If equity is negative, the company owes more than it owns on its books.
u16l3-9.explanation: It's a serious sign, although sometimes it's due to large share buybacks at very profitable companies. You need to look at why.

u16l4-1.prompt: Operating cash flow of €80m and capex of €30m. What's the free cash flow?

u16l4-2.prompt: Free cash flow of €150m and 60 million shares. What's FCF per share?

u16l4-4.prompt: Which part of the cash flow statement does it belong to?
u16l4-4.explanation: Day-to-day business, investments and how the company is financed.

u16l4-5.prompt: Rising profits and negative free cash flow for five years in a row. What does it indicate?
u16l4-5.explanation: The profits aren't turning into real money.

u16l4-8.prompt: A retail chain has negative FCF this year because it has opened 200 shops, but its operating cash flow is high and growing. How do you read it?
options: It doesn't matter, cash isn't important
Alarm: it's about to go bust
It may be reasonable: it's investing to grow, as long as the new shops end up paying off
u16l4-8.explanation: Negative FCF from heavy investment isn't the same as a business that doesn't get paid.
feedback: It does matter, which is why you need to understand the reason.
Not necessarily: FCF is negative because it's investing in growth, not because the business isn't generating cash.
That's it: cash that never arrives isn't the same as cash that gets invested.

u16l4-10.prompt: What can a company do with its free cash flow? Select all that apply.
options: Count it as next year's sales
u16l4-10.explanation: FCF is money available; it isn't a sale.

u16l5-1.prompt: Financial debt of €300m and cash of €100m. What's the net debt?

u16l5-2.prompt: With that net debt of €200m and EBITDA of €100m, what's net debt/EBITDA?
u16l5-2.explanation: 200 ÷ 100 = 2 times: at the edge of comfortable.

u16l5-3.prompt: EBIT of €90m and interest of €30m. What's the interest cover?
u16l5-3.explanation: 90 ÷ 30 = 3 times: tight. If EBIT halves, it barely covers it 1.5 times.

u16l5-6.prompt: Which sector can usually carry more debt without it being worrying?
u16l5-6.explanation: Stable, regulated income makes it possible to service more debt with fewer scares.

u16l5-8.prompt: Industrial company: how does its net debt/EBITDA look?
right: Keep an eye on it (2 to 4)

u16l5-10.prompt: Marta is torn between two companies that are identical except for their debt. A: net debt/EBITDA of 0.5 and ROE of 12 %. B: net debt/EBITDA of 4.5 and ROE of 20 %. What should she bear in mind?
options: That debt doesn't matter if the company makes money
That B is better: its ROE is higher
That B's ROE may be inflated by debt and that it will fare worse in a crisis
u16l5-10.explanation: Look at ROE alongside debt: debt inflates both returns and risk.
feedback: It's making money today; the question is what happens the year it doesn't.
Part of that ROE may come from debt, which also multiplies losses when things go wrong.
That's it: more debt, more risk. It's not a better business, just a more leveraged one.

u16l6-2.prompt: Bruno owns shares in a tech company that reports results tomorrow. He's read they'll be "amazing" and wants to triple his position just beforehand. What is he missing?
options: That tomorrow is a bank holiday
That the price already reflects what's expected and it can open with a gap in either direction
Nothing: if they're amazing, it'll go up
u16l6-2.explanation: Before results, the risk is bigger than it looks: a stop doesn't protect you from a gap.
feedback: That's not the issue: the issue is the risk of a gap.
Good: results day is no time to multiply the size of a position.
If "amazing" is what everyone expects, it's already in the price. And if it disappoints, the gap can be huge.

u16l6-3.prompt: Real chart of a big tech company: 30 sessions with no name or date. What did it do over the next 10?
u16l6-3.explanation: Even if you knew its figures before anyone else, you wouldn't know how the market would react: it depends on what it was expecting.

u16l6-4.prompt: Another real share, another 30 sessions. Up or down?
u16l6-4.explanation: Without knowing what the market expects, the chart alone isn't enough to tell what's coming.

u16l6-6.prompt: A share is at €50 before results and your stop is at €48. It opens with a −12 % gap. At roughly what price is your sale filled?
u16l6-6.explanation: 50 × 0.88 = €44. The stop triggers at the first available price: €4 below what you planned.

u16l6-7.prompt: Match each term with its meaning.
right: What the company forecasts for the coming quarters
A jump between the close and the open with no prices in between
The average of what analysts expect

u16l6-10.prompt: What can move a share on results day? Select all that apply.
options: The forecasts for the coming quarters
u16l6-10.explanation: Anything that changes what the market expects of the future.

u16l7-1.prompt: Put the reading order we suggest in sequence: facts first, then the story.
options: Income statement, balance sheet and cash flows
u16l7-1.explanation: If you read the story with the numbers already in your head, you're far less likely to get carried away.

u16l7-3.prompt: Match each document or source with what it is.
u16l7-3.explanation: Knowing where to look saves hours.
right: Quarterly report of a US company
Detail on debt, lawsuits and accounting policies
Regulator where you can look up Spanish listed companies
Annual report of a US company

u16l7-4.prompt: While you read the report, you look at the share price over the last two months. What trend does it show? (Apple · closes every 3 sessions · February–April 2025)
u16l7-4.explanation: The chart tells you what the price has done; the report, whether the business has changed. A fall with no change in the business isn't the same as a fall because the investment case has broken.

u16l7-5.prompt: "Adjusted" profit is €120m and the official figure is €70m. How many M€ of costs have been set aside as "one-offs"?
u16l7-5.explanation: 120 − 70 = €50m. If that happens every year, they're normal costs.

u16l7-6.prompt: Where do you find the official reports of a US company?

u16l7-10.prompt: If you only have 10 minutes with an annual report, what do you look at? Pick the three most useful.
options: How sales and profit have developed
u16l7-10.explanation: Growth, cash and debt: the essentials in little time.
